skills.title: Build a Rainwater Harvesting Tank
skills.sub: from a food-grade drum and a first-flush diverter
skills.why: A 50 m² roof collects about 400 litres from one 10 mm shower: free water when the mains stops.

steps.title: Seal and test
steps.text: Seal every gap a mosquito could enter. After the next rain, check the first flush filled and the water looks clear.

notes.text: Never drink roof water untreated: boil or chlorinate it first. Open or leaky tanks breed dengue mosquitoes within a week.
Empty the first-flush pipe through its bottom cap after every rain, or it stays full and dirty water flows into the tank.
After 2 weeks there are no wrigglers (larvae) in the tank, and the first-flush pipe is full of brown water after a storm.

skills.drill: Measure your roof, calculate the yield, and fill one drum.

skills.title: Build a Gravity Bucket Water Filter
skills.sub: two buckets, ceramic candles, no power
skills.why: Gravity pushes water through ceramic candles; bacteria and parasites stay on the outside. About 1–4 litres an hour.

notes.text: Most ceramic filters stop bacteria and parasites but NOT viruses or chemicals. After floods, filter and then boil or bleach.
Sand-and-charcoal filters make water look clear, not safe. Use them as a pre-filter only.
Output is clear, the lid never leaks, and flow stays steady for a week.

skills.drill: Build the filter and run 20 litres of tank water through it.

steps.title: Fuse everything
steps.text: A fuse on every positive wire near the battery. Never feed into a wall socket.

notes.text: Feeding an inverter into house wiring without a changeover switch can kill line workers. Electrician only.
Choose LiFePO4 over lead-acid indoors: no gas, about 4× the life, and 80–90% usable.
The controller shows charging in sun, and the battery is full again by late afternoon.

skills.drill: Run your essentials on solar only for one full weekend.

skills.title: Build a Brick Rocket Stove
skills.sub: cook with a handful of sticks when the gas runs out
skills.why: An L-shaped, insulated chimney pulls air through the fire, so it burns hot, clean, and on about half the wood.

steps.title: Cook
steps.text: Set the pot on 3 small spacers so hot gas can escape around the edges. Listen for a steady roar.

notes.text: Outdoors only. Any wood fire in a closed space can build up carbon monoxide, which has no smell and kills in your sleep.
Lots of smoke means wet wood or too many sticks. Use fewer, drier sticks and the smoke almost disappears.
You hear a low roar, flames are pulled sideways into the chimney, and 1 litre of water boils in about 10 minutes.

skills.drill: Boil 1 litre of water on your stove and time it.

skills.title: Keep Cool Without Electricity
skills.sub: stop heat getting in, let hot air out
skills.why: In a power cut, heat exhaustion is a real risk for children and older people. Ventilation and shade do most of the work.

steps.text: Wet cloth on neck and wrists, moving air, regular sips of water.

steps.title: Reflect the roof
steps.text: Long term: light roof paint or reflective foil under the roof cuts heat a lot.

notes.text: Confusion, hot dry skin or fainting in the heat is heat stroke: call 999 and cool the person at once.
Wet cloths over windows cool well in dry places but only a little in humid Miri. Moving air helps more.
Indoor rooms feel cooler than outside by mid-afternoon.

skills.drill: Find which window pair gives the best through-draft in your home.

skills.title: Store Food High, Dry and Sealed
skills.sub: the tropical answer to a root cellar
skills.why: Cellars flood and grow mould here. Shelves above the flood line and airtight buckets keep food safe.

steps.title: Store what you eat
steps.text: Buy 2 extra of what you already eat each week. In 2 months you have 2 weeks spare.

notes.text: Throw out any food or container that sat in flood water, even if it looks sealed.
Strange emergency food gets wasted. Store your family's normal food and rotate it.
Every container is above the flood line, sealed, and dated.

skills.drill: Move your pantry above flood height and date every container.

skills.title: Dry Food in a Solar Dryer
skills.sub: fruit, chilli, fish and herbs
skills.why: Plain sun drying fails in Miri's humidity. A dryer box traps heat and moves air, so food dries in 1–3 days.

steps.title: Store airtight
steps.text: Jar with a silica gel sachet, in the dark.

notes.text: Heat meat and fish to 71 °C before drying. Drying alone doesn't kill germs.
No dryer? An oven at 50–60 °C with the door propped open a finger's width works.
After a week in a jar there are no water drops on the glass.

skills.drill: Dry one batch of banana or pineapple and store it for a month.

skills.title: Salt and Dry Fish (Ikan Masin)
skills.sub: no power needed
skills.why: Salt pulls water out of the fish so germs can't grow. Then drying finishes the job.

steps.title: Soak before cooking
steps.text: Soak in fresh water a few hours, changing the water, to remove extra salt.

notes.text: Soft, slimy or rotten-smelling fish has spoiled. Throw it out.
Fine table salt cakes on the surface. Coarse salt draws water out evenly.
The fish is firm and smells of the sea, with no soft or slimy patches.

skills.drill: Salt and dry 1 kg of small fish.

skills.title: Hot-Smoke Fish (Salai)
skills.sub: brine, dry, smoke, check the temperature
skills.why: Brine seasons and preserves; gentle smoke and heat cook and dry the fish.

steps.title: Watch the smoke
steps.text: Thin blue smoke is right. Thick white smoke makes food bitter.

notes.text: Undercooked smoked fish can carry food poisoning. Always check with a thermometer.
For longer keeping, carry on smoking on low heat until fully firm and dry.
The thermometer reads 63 °C or more in the thickest part.

skills.drill: Smoke two fish and check them with a thermometer.

skills.title: Ferment Vegetables in a Jar
skills.sub: sour mustard greens (jeruk sawi), sauerkraut and more
skills.why: Good bacteria turn sugar into acid. The acid preserves the vegetables for months, with nothing but salt and a jar.

steps.title: Refrigerate
steps.text: When it tastes sour enough, close the lid and move it to the fridge to slow fermentation.

notes.text: Throw it out if you see fuzzy pink, black, blue or green mould, the vegetables go slimy, or it smells rotten rather than sour.
A flat white film on top is usually harmless kahm yeast. Skim it off. Fuzzy and coloured means mould: bin it.
Small bubbles rise from day 1–2, the brine turns cloudy, and it smells clean and sour.

skills.drill: Make one jar of fermented mustard greens.

skills.title: Pickle Vegetables in Vinegar (Acar)
skills.sub: 30 minutes, keeps for a year sealed
skills.why: Vinegar makes the jar too sour for germs. Getting the vinegar strength right is the whole trick.

steps.title: Seal and chill
steps.text: Keep in the fridge, or water-bath (2.6) to store on a shelf.

notes.text: Weak "vinegar flavour" products may be under 5% and won't preserve safely. Check the label.
Slice everything the same thickness so it pickles evenly.
Vegetables stay crisp and the brine stays clear after a week.

skills.drill: Make one jar of acar.

skills.title: Can Food in Jars Safely
skills.sub: the one preserving method you must get right
skills.why: Done wrong, canning can grow botulism, which you can't see, smell or taste. Low-acid food needs a pressure canner.

steps.title: Check every seal
steps.text: Press the lid centre: no flex = sealed. Bulging lids: throw away unopened.

notes.text: A boiling pot only reaches 100 °C; botulism spores survive. Low-acid food needs about 116 °C in a pressure canner.
Use only tested recipes and times (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning).
Every lid is sealed and doesn't flex, and each jar is labelled with contents and date.

steps.text: 2 cups flour, ¾ cup water, pinch of salt, 1 tbsp oil. Knead, rest 20 min, roll thin, very hot dry pan.

steps.title: Stock
steps.text: Bones and scraps covered with water, simmer 3–6 hours, strain.

notes.text: Stock is low-acid: freeze it or pressure-can it, never water-bath can it.
In Miri's heat, feed the starter twice a day.
Flatbread puffs on the pan; the rice is fluffy with no burnt base.

skills.drill: Make flatbread on a pan, and rice in a pot without a rice cooker.

skills.title: Light a Fire, Even in the Wet
skills.sub: tinder, kindling, fuel and a tipi lay
skills.why: Most fires fail because the builder runs out of small fuel. Collect everything first, then light once.

steps.title: Feed gradually
steps.text: More kindling, then thicker wood once it burns strongly. Don't smother it.

notes.text: Never use petrol to start or revive a fire. It flashes into a fireball.
Dead branches still on the tree are drier than wood on the ground. Split sticks to reach the dry core.
Fire lit from one flame or spark, burning wrist-thick wood within 10 minutes.

skills.drill: Light a fire with a ferro rod after rain, using only material found on site.

skills.title: Rig a Hammock and Tarp Shelter
skills.sub: off the ground and under a roof
skills.why: In the Borneo forest the ground is wet and full of ants and leeches. Get up off it and under cover.

steps.title: Net and drip lines
steps.text: Close the mosquito net. Tie short strings on the hammock ropes so rain drips off there.

notes.text: Look up before you hang anything. Falling dead branches kill campers every year.
Lie diagonally across the hammock: you'll lie almost flat.
You stay dry through a 10-minute hosepipe test, and no part of the tarp touches the hammock.

skills.drill: Set up the shelter in your garden in under 15 minutes, then sleep in it one night.

skills.title: Make Water Safe to Drink
skills.sub: clear it first, then disinfect
skills.why: Dirty water causes diarrhoea, which kills by dehydration. After floods it's the biggest everyday health risk.

steps.title: Flood water: last resort
steps.text: It can carry fuel and chemicals that nothing here removes. Use stored water first.

notes.text: Never use scented, colour-safe or detergent bleach. The label should say plain sodium hypochlorite.
Bleached water should smell faintly of chlorine after 30 minutes. No smell? Dose again and wait 15 minutes.
The water is clear, has been treated by one method, and smells faintly of chlorine if bleached.

skills.drill: Treat 1 litre each by boiling, bleach and SODIS. Taste all three.

skills.title: Five Knots for Almost Every Job
skills.sub: what each one is for; watch them tied slowly at animatedknots.com
skills.why: With these five you can hang a tarp, strap a load to a car, join two ropes and make a rescue loop.

steps.title: Practise blind
steps.text: Tie each knot 10 times with your eyes closed.

notes.text: Never trust a knot you haven't tested with your full weight before using it to hold a person.
Learn with two colours of rope. Seeing which end does what is half the battle.
You can tie all five blindfolded, and the bowline holds your weight from a branch.

skills.drill: Tie all five blindfolded, 10 times each.

skills.title: Find Your Way Without GPS
skills.sub: map, compass, sun, shadow and stars
skills.why: Near the equator the sun is almost overhead at midday, so use mornings, afternoons and the stars.

steps.title: Lost? STOP
steps.text: Sit, think, observe, plan. Usually stay put; if you must move, follow water downstream.

notes.text: Don't push on when lost at dusk. Stop, make shelter and signal (3.6); search teams look in daylight.
Polaris sits only about 4° above the horizon in Miri, often hidden by trees. Use Orion instead.
Your shadow-stick north matches your phone compass within about 20°.

skills.drill: Find north with a shadow stick and check it against your phone compass.

skills.title: Signal for Rescue
skills.sub: sound, light, symbols and smoke
skills.why: Rescuers spot contrast, movement and things in threes. Make yourself big, bright and repeated.

steps.title: Mirror flash
steps.text: Make a V with your fingers around the aircraft, tilt the mirror so the light spot sits in the V.

steps.title: Ground symbols
steps.text: Letters 3 m or taller in a clearing: V = need help, X = need medical help, SOS.

steps.title: Phone
steps.text: No signal? Send a text anyway; texts often get through. Save battery for emergencies.

notes.text: Keep signal fires small and controlled. A forest fire makes everything worse.
Carry the whistle on a cord round your neck. Shouting tires you in minutes; a whistle carries further.
You can hit a target 50 m away with a mirror flash.

skills.drill: Hit a target 50 m away with a mirror flash (use a CD if you have no mirror).

skills.title: Sharpen a Knife or Parang
skills.sub: whetstone, angle, burr and strop
skills.why: A sharp blade is safer than a blunt one: it cuts where you aim instead of slipping.

steps.title: Strop and test
steps.text: Strop spine-first on leather, then slice paper. Clean cut = sharp.

notes.text: Always stroke away from your fingers, and keep the free hand flat on the blade's spine side.
Colour the edge with a marker. If the ink wears off evenly, your angle is right.
The blade slices printer paper cleanly without tearing.

skills.drill: Sharpen every kitchen knife until each passes the paper test.

skills.title: Build a Home First-Aid Kit
skills.sub: everything for cuts, burns, fever and dehydration, in one box
skills.why: A kit nobody can find in 30 seconds is useless. One bright box, one known place, checked twice a year.

steps.title: One place, checked
steps.text: Same spot, everyone knows it. Check expiry dates every 6 months.

notes.text: Add a tourniquet (7.3). Life-threatening bleeding needs one; a kit without it can't stop the worst injuries.
Tape a list of contents inside the lid and tick off what you use, so you know what to restock.
Anyone at home can fetch the kit in under 30 seconds and name what's inside.

skills.drill: Assemble the kit and show everyone at home where it lives.

skills.title: Mix a Rehydration Drink (ORS)
skills.sub: the WHO home recipe for diarrhoea and dehydration
skills.why: Diarrhoea drains water and salts. The right mix of sugar and salt helps the gut absorb water; plain water alone can't.

steps.title: Sip small, often
steps.text: A few sips every minute or two; a cup after each loose stool. Make it fresh every 24 hours.

notes.text: Go to a clinic if there's blood in the stool, no urine for 8+ hours, sunken eyes, confusion, or a baby with dry nappies.
Keep ready-made ORS sachets in the kit: they're more accurate than home measuring.
It tastes like slightly salty, slightly sweet water, and the person is passing pale urine again.

skills.drill: Make one litre and taste it so you know what right tastes like.

skills.title: Clean and Dress a Wound
skills.sub: cuts, scrapes and grazes that don't need stitches
skills.why: Plenty of clean running water does more to prevent infection than any antiseptic. Infection is fast in the tropics.

steps.title: Watch for 3 days
steps.text: Spreading redness, red streaks, pus or fever means see a doctor.

notes.text: Bites, deep punctures, gaping cuts, or any cut from flood or river water: see a doctor (tetanus, leptospirosis).
Check your tetanus jab date. Adults need a booster about every 10 years.
After 3 days the edges are pink, not red and spreading, and there's no pus.

skills.drill: Dress a pretend wound on a family member's forearm.

skills.title: Treat a Burn
skills.sub: the 20-minute rule, and what never to put on a burn
skills.why: Cooling with running water for 20 minutes is the single most effective burn treatment, even up to 3 hours later.

steps.title: Hospital for these
steps.text: Face, hands, feet, groin, joints, deep or charred burns, and all burns on babies.

notes.text: Chemical and electrical burns always need hospital, even if they look small.
Don't burst blisters. They protect the skin underneath from infection.
The pain eases while cooling and the burn is covered loosely, not wrapped.

skills.drill: Set a 20-minute timer with your hand under the tap, to learn how long it really is.

skills.title: Natural Remedies: What Works
skills.sub: an honest scorecard
skills.why: Fine for comfort. Never a replacement for medical care when there are danger signs.

steps.text: Doesn't replace antibiotics. Don't rely on it for infections.

steps.title: Turmeric
steps.text: Mixed evidence for joint pain and poorly absorbed. Harmless in food.

notes.text: Herbs can interact with prescription medicines. Ask a pharmacist if you take regular medication.
Honey (1–2 tsp before bed) helps coughs in children over 1 and adults.
You use remedies for comfort only, and see a doctor when danger signs appear.

skills.drill: Grow one aloe vera plant at home.

skills.title: Tropical Illness Red Flags
skills.sub: dengue, leptospirosis and heat illness
skills.why: With dengue the danger often comes as the fever drops, not at its peak. Knowing the warning signs saves lives.

steps.title: Heat stroke
steps.text: Confused or collapsed in the heat: call 999 and cool fast with water and fanning.

notes.text: Heat stroke and severe dengue are emergencies. Don't wait to see if they improve.
Get a blood test (full blood count) at a clinic from day 2–3 of any high fever during dengue season.
Everyone at home knows: fever means paracetamol only, and which signs mean hospital.

skills.drill: Save your nearest clinic and hospital emergency numbers in your phone and on paper.

skills.title: Hand-Sew: Three Stitches and a Button
skills.sub: repairs that save you money every month
skills.why: With a running stitch, a backstitch, a whip stitch and a proper button shank you can fix almost any clothing.

steps.title: Button with a shank
steps.text: Pin across the button as a spacer, 6–8 passes, remove pin, wrap 5× underneath, knot.

notes.text: Keep needles in a closed tin, away from children.
Sew with doubled thread for buttons; single thread for seams.
A backstitched seam doesn't open when you pull hard on both sides.

skills.drill: Sew a button with a shank and repair one split seam with backstitch.

skills.title: Fix Basic Plumbing
skills.sub: stopcock, dripping tap, running toilet, blocked sink
skills.why: Most household leaks and blockages need a washer, a plunger and ten minutes, not a plumber.

steps.text: Water off, unscrew the handle and headgear, replace the washer. Take the old one to the shop.

steps.text: Water spilling into the overflow? Lower the float. Leaking into the bowl? Replace the seal.

steps.title: Clear the U-bend
steps.text: Bucket underneath, unscrew both nuts by hand, clean out, refit hand-tight.

notes.text: Avoid caustic drain cleaners: they burn skin and damage pipes.
Photograph each part as you take it apart so you can put it back in order.
No drips after an hour, and the sink drains freely.

skills.drill: Find and turn your stopcock, then remove and clean one sink U-bend.

skills.title: Electrical Basics, Safely
skills.sub: what to do yourself and where to stop
skills.why: Knowing your distribution board turns a scary blackout into a 2-minute fix, and tells you when to call an electrician.

steps.title: Know your limit
steps.text: Plugs and bulbs with the power off: fine. Inside the board or new wiring: electrician.

notes.text: Never switch power back on after a flood until an electrician has checked the wiring.
Keep a torch clipped beside the board for blackouts.
Every breaker is labelled and the RCCB trips when tested.

skills.drill: Label your breakers and press the RCCB test button.

skills.title: Make Bar Soap
skills.sub: cold process, with lye handled safely
skills.why: Oils plus lye make soap. The lye is dangerous until it reacts, so gear and the right order matter most.

steps.text: Always pour lye INTO water, outdoors. Never water into lye. Cool to about 40 °C.

steps.title: Cut and cure
steps.text: Cut into bars and cure on a rack for 4–6 weeks before use.

notes.text: Lye causes severe chemical burns and blindness. If it touches skin, rinse under running water for 15 minutes.
Not ready for lye? Melt-and-pour glycerin soap base needs no dangerous chemicals.
Cured bars are hard and don't sting when you touch them with a wet finger.

skills.drill: Make one batch of melt-and-pour soap, then a cold-process batch with goggles on.

skills.title: Light Without Power
skills.sub: candles, oil lamps, and why LED is better
skills.why: Flames cause house fires during blackouts. Use them as a backup to LED lanterns, never a first choice.

steps.title: Never unattended
steps.text: Put out every flame before you leave the room or sleep.

notes.text: Keep matches, lighters and candles out of children's reach.
An oil lamp burns cleaner than a candle and for hours on a cup of oil.
The lamp burns steadily with little smoke.

skills.drill: Make one jar oil lamp and time how long it burns.

skills.title: Look After a Generator
skills.sub: 15 minutes a month keeps it ready
skills.why: A generator that hasn't run in months often won't start when you need it.

steps.title: Outdoors, 6 m away
steps.text: At least 6 m from doors and windows, exhaust pointing away.

notes.text: Never run a generator indoors, in a garage, under the house or on a porch. Carbon monoxide kills.
Write each run date on a log taped to the generator.
It starts first or second pull every month.

skills.drill: Run the generator this month and log the date.

skills.title: Money and Documents
skills.sub: when cards and ATMs stop working
skills.why: Power cuts take down ATMs and card machines. A little cash and sealed documents keep you moving.

steps.title: Skills as currency
steps.text: After a disaster, fixing a pump or dressing a wound is worth more than a stockpile.

notes.text: Don't keep all your cash in one place, and never tell strangers you keep cash at home.
Put the document bag inside the go-bag (7.6) so it leaves with you.
You could pay for food and fuel for a week with no card or phone.

skills.drill: Photograph all key documents and seal the originals in a waterproof bag.

skills.title: What to Grow in Miri
skills.sub: fast greens to long-term calories
skills.why: Plant some quick greens, some medium crops and some long-term calories so something is always ready.

steps.title: Banana
steps.text: Fruit in 9–12 months, then keeps producing through side shoots.

notes.text: Raw or undercooked cassava contains cyanide compounds. Peel, soak and cook thoroughly.
Chilli, ginger, turmeric, lemongrass and pandan grow well in pots on a balcony.
You harvest something every week from month 2.

skills.drill: Grow sweet potato and kangkung for one season and record the harvest.

skills.title: Build a Raised Bed for Heavy Rain
skills.sub: drainage, acid soil and monsoon cover
skills.why: Height drains heavy rain away from the roots; mulch stops rain splashing fungus onto leaves.

skills.drill: Start a covered compost heap and turn it on schedule for 6 weeks.

skills.title: Save Seeds and Control Pests Naturally
skills.sub: free seed every season, fewer chemicals
skills.why: Seeds from open-pollinated plants grow true year after year. Neem and netting handle most pests.

notes.text: Even natural sprays can irritate. Wash produce before eating.
Easiest seeds to start with: long beans, chilli, tomato, okra, pumpkin.
Saved seeds germinate next season.

skills.drill: Save one jar of chilli or bean seeds and replant them next season.

skills.title: Small Livestock and Aquaponics
skills.sub: eggs, fish and greens together
skills.why: A few hens give eggs daily; fish in a tank can fertilise vegetables in an aquaponics loop.

steps.text: Fish waste feeds the grow bed; plants clean water for the fish. Needs a pump.

steps.title: Check the rules
steps.text: Ask your local council before keeping poultry in housing areas.

notes.text: The aquaponics pump needs power. Back it up with solar (1.3) or fish can die in a long cut.
4–6 hens give about 3–5 eggs a day.
Hens are laying and fish are growing after 2 months.

skills.drill: Visit a local aquaponics or chicken setup and ask about costs and problems.

skills.title: Give CPR to an Adult
skills.sub: when someone collapses and isn't breathing normally
skills.why: Without CPR, survival drops with every minute. You can't make it worse: pushing hard keeps blood moving to the brain until help arrives.

steps.title: Check breathing: 10 s
steps.text: Look at the chest, listen and feel at the mouth for up to 10 seconds. Gasping is not breathing.

steps.text: Heel of hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top, arms straight. 30 pushes, 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 a minute.

steps.title: Give 2 breaths
steps.text: Tilt the head, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs, blow for 1 second twice. Can't or won't? Just keep pushing.

steps.title: Use the AED
steps.text: Switch it on and do exactly what the voice says. Keep pushing until it tells you to stand clear.

notes.text: Occasional gasping or snoring is NOT normal breathing. Treat it as no breathing and start pushing.
Push to the beat of "Stayin' Alive" (about 104 a minute). Swap with someone every 2 minutes so you don't tire.
On a course manikin, the clicker or light confirms correct depth and rate for 2 full minutes.

skills.drill: Complete a certified CPR + AED course (St John Ambulance or Red Crescent).

skills.title: Clear a Choking Airway
skills.sub: adults and children over 1 year
skills.why: A blocked airway kills in minutes. Five firm back blows, then five thrusts, repeated, clears most blockages.

steps.text: If they can still cough, tell them to cough hard. Stay with them.

steps.title: 5 back blows
steps.text: Lean them forward, support the chest. Hit firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

steps.title: 5 abdominal thrusts
steps.text: Stand behind, fist just above the navel, other hand over it. Pull sharply in and up.

steps.text: Lower them down, call 999 and start CPR (7.1).

notes.text: Babies under 1: never give abdominal thrusts. Use back blows and two-finger chest thrusts; learn this on a course.
Anyone who needed abdominal thrusts should see a doctor afterwards, even if they feel fine.
The person can breathe, speak and cough normally again.

skills.drill: Walk a partner through the hand positions slowly. Never thrust for real on someone who isn't choking.

skills.title: Stop Severe Bleeding
skills.sub: direct pressure, wound packing and a tourniquet
skills.why: A person can bleed to death in 3–5 minutes. Hard pressure stops most bleeding; a tourniquet stops the rest on arms and legs.

steps.text: Groin, armpit or neck: stuff gauze tightly into the wound, then press hard for at least 3 minutes.

steps.title: Keep them warm
steps.text: Lie them down, cover with a blanket and keep talking until help arrives.

notes.text: Belts and cloth rarely get tight enough to work as tourniquets. Buy a real one.
Practise putting the tourniquet on your own arm, one-handed, until you can do it in under 30 seconds.
Bleeding stops completely and you can't feel a pulse below the tourniquet.

skills.drill: Apply a real tourniquet to your own arm one-handed in under 30 seconds (release it straight after).

skills.title: Snakebite First Aid
skills.sub: what to do, and the old tricks that make it worse
skills.why: Most bites are survivable with antivenom at a hospital. Your job is to keep the person still and get them there fast.

steps.title: Hospital, fast
steps.text: Note the bite time. A photo of the snake from a safe distance helps doctors.

notes.text: Don't let the person walk if you can carry or drive them. Every step spreads venom.
Save your nearest hospital's emergency number in your phone now, before you need it.
The person is still, splinted and on the way to hospital within minutes.

skills.drill: Practise splinting a partner's leg with a stick and strips of cloth.

skills.title: Get Through a Flood
skills.sub: the most likely emergency in Miri: before, during and after
skills.why: Most flood deaths happen to people walking or driving through moving water. Leaving early is the single biggest life-saver.

steps.title: Bin food, check wiring
steps.text: Throw out any food flood water touched. An electrician checks wiring before power goes back on.

notes.text: Turn around, don't drown. Never walk or drive through moving flood water, however shallow it looks.
Photograph the damage for insurance before you start cleaning.
Your family knows the route to high ground and the go-bags are by the door before November.

skills.drill: Walk or drive your evacuation route to high ground with the family.

skills.title: Pack a 72-Hour Go-Bag
skills.sub: one bag per person, ready to grab in 10 minutes
skills.why: In an evacuation you won't have time to think. A packed bag means water, light, medicine and documents leave with you.

steps.title: Pack and test
steps.text: Add clothes, poncho, whistle, multi-tool. Time a leave-in-10-minutes test.

notes.text: Medicines expire and power banks go flat. Check the bag every October before the monsoon.
A sarong is the most useful single item: blanket, towel, sling, sunshade and privacy screen.
Everyone can grab their bag and be out of the door in under 10 minutes.

skills.drill: Pack one go-bag per person and do a leave-in-10-minutes test.

skills.title: Plan for a Long Power Cut
skills.sub: water, light, cooking, food and contact for 7 days
skills.why: A long blackout is uncomfortable, not deadly, if you've planned. Fill in each step as a family.

steps.title: Family meeting plan
steps.text: Agree a meeting point and one out-of-town contact everyone calls.

notes.text: Carbon monoxide from charcoal, gas heaters or generators indoors kills families in power cuts every year.
Keep a few bottles of frozen water in the freezer: they keep it cold longer and become drinking water.
Everyone in the family can say where to meet and who to call.

skills.drill: Write the family plan on one page and stick it on the fridge.

skills.title: Negotiate a Fair Deal
skills.sub: at work, at the market, with contractors
skills.why: The person with the stronger walk-away option usually gets the better deal.

steps.title: Write it down
steps.text: End with a short written summary, even a WhatsApp message.

notes.text: Never agree under time pressure you didn't create. "Let me sleep on it" is always allowed.
Practise on small purchases first.
You walked away with your key points and the other side still wants to deal again.

skills.drill: Negotiate one real purchase this month using steps 1–4.

skills.title: Read People: Myths and Reality
skills.sub: what body language can and can't tell you
skills.why: No gesture proves anything. Changes from someone's normal behaviour, in clusters, are what matter.

steps.title: Look for clusters
steps.text: Crossed arms alone mean nothing. Crossed arms + turned away + short answers is a signal.

steps.text: Avoiding eye contact or fidgeting doesn't prove lying; even trained people barely beat chance.

steps.title: Ask for detail
steps.text: Ask for specifics and see whether the story stays consistent over time.

notes.text: Don't accuse people based on body language. It's unreliable and damages trust.
Open questions ("tell me about…") reveal more than yes/no questions.
You base judgements on what people say and do over time, not one gesture.

skills.drill: In your next meeting, notice one person's baseline before anything important is discussed.

skills.title: Calm an Angry Person
skills.sub: de-escalation step by step
skills.why: Anger drops when people feel heard and safe. Your voice and distance do most of the work.

steps.text: Don't argue facts while they're angry. "We can sort it here, or I'll get the manager."

steps.title: Leave if needed
steps.text: Weapon or violence: leave and call 999.

notes.text: Your safety comes first. Pride is never worth staying in a dangerous situation.
Lower your own volume when they raise theirs.
Their voice drops and they start talking about solutions.

skills.drill: Practise the steps by role-play with a friend.

skills.title: Six Levers of Persuasion
skills.sub: use them honestly, spot them when they're used on you
skills.why: Based on Robert Cialdini's research. Naming the lever takes away most of its power.

steps.title: Scarcity
steps.text: Honest: true deadlines. Watch for fake countdowns and "only 2 left".

notes.text: The ad that sells this book uses scarcity and fear. Pause before buying under pressure.
When you feel rushed, ask: which lever is being pulled right now?
You can name the lever in any advert you see.

skills.drill: Find all six levers in one week of adverts.

skills.title: Situational Awareness
skills.sub: a habit, not a skill you learn once
skills.why: Most danger can be avoided by noticing it early. Relaxed but aware is the state to live in.

Make exit-spotting a game with children: who finds it first?
You can name two exits in every building you enter today.

skills.why: In a real emergency, the people next door arrive long before help does.

steps.title: Flood buddies
steps.text: Agree who checks on whom and where to meet.

notes.text: Keep the shared list private to the street; it contains personal details.
Start with one small gathering: food brings people together.
Every vulnerable neighbour has a named buddy.

skills.drill: Start or join your street's emergency group and assign a buddy to each vulnerable neighbour.

foot: Educational reference. Safety points follow WHO, CDC and USDA guidance as summarised in the main field manual; check current versions before relying on them.
